usage: Do you have time, by any chance?
softens a request to a near-stranger
Where is the restroom, by chance?
Are you Korean, by any chance?
a careful guess, not an assumption
fixed phrase, stands on its own
examples: 혹시 이거 얼마예요?
How much is this, by any chance?
Drop 혹시 at the very front; it instantly makes a blunt question gentle.
혹시 영어 할 수 있는 분 계세요?
Is there anyone who can speak English, by chance?
계세요 (honorific of 있어요) plus 혹시 makes this a soft, respectful ask to a room.
우산 챙기세요, 혹시 모르니까요.
Bring an umbrella, just in case.
Here 혹시 모르니까 = 'because you never know' — the just-in-case use, not a question.
nuance: 혹시 is the Sino-Korean 或是 (或 'perhaps' + 是 'be so') and lives at the FRONT of a question to soften it, exactly like English 'by any chance' or 'do you happen to': it signals you are unsure and refuse to assume, so requests and guesses land politely rather than pushily. Do not confuse it with 만약 (萬若, 'if / supposing'): 만약 sets up a conditional clause and pairs with -면 (만약 비가 오면 = if it rains), whereas 혹시 colors a whole question with tentativeness and does NOT need -면. The big English-speaker trap is dropping 혹시 into a flat statement; it belongs with a question or with the set phrase 혹시 몰라서 / 혹시 모르니까 ('just in case'). It also collocates with 혹시나 (an even softer, more anxious variant) and with 혹시 ~ 거 아니에요? for a worried hunch.

examples: 설마 벌써 다 팔렸어요?
No way, is it already sold out?
Front-loaded 설마 turns a plain question into 'don't tell me...' disbelief.
설마 비 오는데 안 가는 건 아니죠?
Surely you're not skipping it just because it's raining?
설마 ... 아니죠? is the classic frame: it fishes for the answer 'no, of course not'.
설마 했는데 진짜였어요.
I figured it couldn't be, but it was true.
설마 했는데 = 'I thought surely not, and yet' — the let-down twist.
nuance: 설마 expresses strong disbelief that something bad or shocking could actually be true — 'surely not', 'you've got to be kidding', 'don't tell me'. Crucially it ANTICIPATES a denial: the speaker wants the answer to be no, which is why it loves the frames 설마 ~ 아니죠? and 설마 그럴 리가 없다. Contrast it sharply with 아마 (probably): 아마 is a neutral, fairly confident guess that something IS so (아마 올 거예요 = he'll probably come), whereas 설마 leans the opposite way, hoping it is NOT so. The English-speaker pitfall is using 설마 for ordinary 'maybe', or for guesses you actually expect to be true — that is 아마 or 어쩌면. Also remember 설마 carries emotion (alarm, dread, incredulity), so it is out of place in a calm, factual statement. The frozen reply 설마요 alone means 'no way, really?'.

usage: please, I hope it's not today
examples: 제발 조용히 해 주세요.
Please be quiet, I'm begging you.
Said when 조용히 해 주세요 alone isn't strong enough — 제발 adds real desperation.
제발 비가 안 왔으면 좋겠어요.
I really hope it doesn't rain.
제발 + the -았/었으면 좋겠다 wish frame: pleading with fate, not a person.
제발 한 번만 봐주세요.
Please let it slide just this once.
봐주다 = 'go easy / let off'; 제발 한 번만 is the earnest 'just this once' plea.
nuance: 제발 is a heartfelt, emotionally loaded 'please' used when you are genuinely pleading or desperate — far stronger than the bare polite ending -주세요, which is just normal courtesy. Think of -주세요 as everyday 'please pass the salt', and 제발 as 'I am begging you'. Because it carries real feeling, Koreans reserve it for moments that truly matter (제발 살려 주세요, 제발 그만해), and it can sound melodramatic or even rude if sprinkled on trivial requests. It pairs naturally with 좀 (제발 좀...) to intensify, with 부탁이다 ('it's a request'), and with wish endings -았으면 좋겠다 when you are pleading with circumstances rather than a person. The English-speaker trap is treating 제발 like the all-purpose English 'please' that politely tags every request — in Korean that politeness job is done by -주세요 / -ㄹ게요, and overusing 제발 makes you sound frantic.

Pairing 제발 with a cold command and no softening — it usually goes with -주세요, 좀, or a wish ending (제발 ~았으면 좋겠어요), matching its emotional tone.

english: just in time; as it happens
usage: you came at just the right time
as it happens, I have time
I happen to be going that way too
examples: 마침 버스가 와서 안 기다렸어요.
The bus came just then, so I didn't wait.
Basic use: 마침 marks the happy 'right at that moment' timing before the verb.
마침 세일하길래 하나 샀어요.
It happened to be on sale, so I bought one.
마침 + -길래 ('since it happened to...') is a very natural cause frame for lucky chance.
전화하려던 참인데 마침 연락이 왔어요.
I was about to call, and just then they reached out.
-던 참인데 + 마침 stacks two 'right at that instant' cues for a perfect coincidence.
nuance: 마침 marks a lucky, convenient coincidence — 'just in time', 'as it happens', 'right then' — framing an event as a happy accident that fell into place rather than something planned. Do NOT confuse it with 드디어 ('finally / at last'), which is about a long-awaited thing arriving after waiting (드디어 끝났다 = it's finally over); 마침 has no sense of waiting, only of fortunate timing. Its true opposite is 하필, the ANNOYING coincidence: where 마침 is good luck, 하필 is bad luck, so never use 마침 for an unfortunate clash. It collocates with 마침 잘됐다 ('that worked out perfectly'), 마침 잘 왔다 ('you came at the right time'), and the cause endings -길래 / -아서. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 'finally' (드디어) when you mean 'as luck would have it', or using 마침 for a bad coincidence that should be 하필.

Using 마침 for a BAD coincidence — an unlucky clash is 하필 (하필 그날 비가 왔다); 마침 is reserved for timing that helps you.
Treating 마침 as 'exactly/precisely' for measurements — that is 정확히/딱; 마침 specifically frames a convenient coincidence of timing.

english: of all times; why this one
usage: sits in front of a noun
why right now of all times?
of all days it rained that day
of all things / of all people
examples: 하필 약속 날에 몸이 아팠어요.
Of all days, I got sick on the day of the plans.
하필 + 날 spotlights the cruel timing — the worst possible day.
왜 하필 나한테 그래요?
Why me, of all people?
왜 하필 나... is the set complaint: 'out of everyone, why ME?'
하필이면 비 오는 날 우산을 안 가져왔어요.
Of all days, I forgot my umbrella the day it rained.
하필이면 (emphatic) drives home just how unlucky the choice of day was.
nuance: 하필 voices frustration at unlucky, badly chosen timing or circumstance — 'of all times', 'why this one in particular', 'just my luck'. It is the negative twin of 마침: 마침 is the lucky coincidence, 하필 is the maddening one, so they are not interchangeable. It is built on the Sino-Korean 何必 (何 'what' + 必 'necessarily') — literally 'why must it be (this)?' — which is exactly the grumbling rhetorical question it carries, and the emphatic 하필이면 stresses how rotten the choice of time, place, or person feels. It collocates with question words (왜 하필...?) and with bad-luck nouns (하필 그날, 하필 시험 날). The English-speaker pitfall is using 하필 for good fortune (that is 마침), or stripping out its complaining, put-upon tone and treating it as neutral 'just then' — 하필 always grumbles.

Flattening its tone to a neutral 'at that time' — 하필 inherently complains ('of all times!'); without that grumble it sounds wrong.
Misreading the 何必 origin as a real 'why must' question needing an answer — here it is a rhetorical sigh of bad luck, usually with no expected reply.

english: after a long while; for once
usage: sits in front of a noun
we met after a long time
examples: 모처럼 친구를 만나서 신났어요.
I was thrilled to see my friend after so long.
모처럼 frames the reunion as rare and therefore special.
모처럼 쉬는 날인데 비가 와요.
It's a rare day off, but it's raining.
The very common bittersweet use: a precious chance spoiled by 비가 와요.
모처럼 왔으니까 맛있는 거 먹어요.
Since we're out for once, let's eat something good.
모처럼 ... -으니까 = 'since this is a rare chance, let's make the most of it'.
nuance: 모처럼 marks something that happens rarely and is therefore precious — 'after a long while', 'for once', 'on this rare occasion' — adding the feeling 'this doesn't come often, so let's value it', and it very often sets up a slight let-down (a rare day off that gets rained out). Compare it with 오랜만에, which also means 'after a long time' but is purely neutral about elapsed time (오랜만에 비가 온다 = it's been a while since it rained — could be good OR bad); 모처럼 carries an extra warmth and the sense of a welcome, scarce opportunity, so 모처럼 비가 온다 would sound odd unless the rain is genuinely wished-for. It collocates with 모처럼의 + noun (모처럼의 휴가 = a rare vacation) and with reason endings -는데 / -으니까 to justify seizing the moment. The English-speaker pitfall is using 모처럼 for ordinary, routine happenings, or treating it as a flat synonym of 오랜만에 — 모처럼 always implies the event is rare AND treasured.

mistakes: Using 모처럼 for everyday routine events — it specifically marks something RARE and welcome (모처럼 쉬는 날), not your daily commute.

Forgetting the 의 when modifying a noun directly — 'a rare opportunity' is 모처럼의 기회, not 모처럼 기회.

usage: this is the little that's left
examples: 늦었지만 그나마 막차를 탔어요.
I was late, but at least I caught the last train.
그나마 flags the one redeeming part of an otherwise bad situation.
월급은 적지만 그나마 야근이 없어요.
The pay is low, but at least there's no overtime.
Sets a downside (적지만) against a small consolation introduced by 그나마.
그나마 네가 있어서 다행이야.
At least I have you, thank goodness.
그나마 ... 다행이다 — relief that, amid hardship, this one good thing remains.
nuance: 그나마 points to a small consolation inside an otherwise bad or limited situation — 'at least', 'even that little bit', 'if nothing else, there's this'. It quietly admits things are not good while spotlighting the single redeeming scrap, so it pairs constantly with 다행이다 (그나마 다행이에요 = 'at least that's a relief'). Contrast it with 그래도 ('still / even so / nevertheless'): 그래도 concedes a point and pushes on regardless (비싸지만 그래도 살래요 = it's pricey but I'll buy it anyway), whereas 그나마 specifically picks out a meager upside as the best of a poor lot. There is also 그것도 vs 그나마도: 그나마도 없다 means 'not even that little bit is left', the bottom of the barrel. The English-speaker pitfall is using 그나마 when the situation is actually fully positive — it requires a backdrop of hardship or scarcity; on genuinely good news it sounds grudging and wrong.

Forgetting the emphatic 그나마도 — 'not even that much' is 그나마도 없어요, with 도 stressing that the last small bit is gone too.

usage: a hedged outcome with -ㄹ 수도 있다
examples: 어쩌면 이번 주말에 시간이 날 수도 있어요.
Maybe I'll have some free time this weekend.
어쩌면 + -ㄹ 수도 있다 keeps the possibility open and uncommitted.
어쩌면 우리 전에 만난 적 있을지도 몰라요.
Maybe we've met somewhere before.
어쩌면 floats a half-formed hunch; -ㄹ지도 몰라요 is its natural partner ending.
어쩌면 그 사람 말이 맞을지도 몰라요.
Maybe that person is right after all.
Signals genuine openness to being wrong — a reconsidering 'maybe'.
nuance: 어쩌면 means 'maybe / possibly' and opens a genuine but uncertain possibility, often one the speaker had not fully considered until now — there's a reflective, 'come to think of it, perhaps...' flavor. It is grammatically drawn to the guessing endings -ㄹ지도 모르다 and -ㄹ 수도 있다, which carry the uncertainty through to the verb. Contrast it with 아마 ('probably'): 아마 is a fairly confident lean toward yes (아마 맞을 거예요 = it's probably right), while 어쩌면 is more open-ended and less committed, weighing a real but not-likely chance, and it can even introduce a surprising or contrary idea. (Note 어쩌면 also has a separate exclamatory use, '어쩌면 이렇게...!' = 'how on earth so...!', but the adverb of possibility is the core meaning here.) The English-speaker pitfall is treating 어쩌면 as confidently as 아마, or pairing it with a flat assertion — it needs a hedging ending, not a bare statement of fact.

Forgetting its reflective 'come to think of it' nuance — it often raises a possibility newly considered, not a settled prediction.

english: as many as; no less than
usage: for no less than ten years
examples: 그 가방이 무려 삼백만 원이에요.
That bag costs a whopping three million won.
무려 right before the figure signals 'shockingly, that much'.
줄을 무려 두 시간이나 섰어요.
I stood in line for a full two hours.
무려 ... -이나 doubles the emphasis on the surprisingly large quantity.
이 영화를 무려 천만 명이 봤어요.
No less than ten million people saw this movie.
Pairs a big round number with 무려 to stress an impressive scale.
nuance: 무려 goes directly before a number or quantity to stress that the amount is surprisingly, impressively large — 'a whopping', 'no less than', 'as many as' — broadcasting that the speaker finds the figure striking or hard to believe. It works ONLY with quantities (money, counts, durations, multiples), never with a general statement, and it loves to combine with the emphatic particle -이나/나 on the number (무려 두 시간이나). Contrast it with 약 (約, 'approximately / about'), which does the opposite job — softening a number into a rough estimate (약 백 명 = about a hundred); 무려 amplifies and dramatizes, 약 hedges and rounds. The English-speaker pitfall is leaving out the number (무려 비싸요 is wrong — say 무려 삼백만 원이에요), or confusing the amplifying 무려 with the estimating 약. If you want plain 'about', reach for 약 or 대략; if you want 'can you believe how much', that's 무려.

examples: 그 식당은 맛있고, 심지어 가격도 싸요.
That restaurant is tasty, and on top of that it's cheap.
심지어 adds an extra, almost too-good point; note 도 on 가격.
비가 오는데 심지어 우산도 없었어요.
It was raining, and I didn't even have an umbrella.
Escalates from bad to worse; 심지어 + 우산도 = 'didn't even have'.
그 사람은 심지어 내 이름도 기억 못 해요.
That person doesn't even remember my name.
Pushes to an extreme case — of all things, not even the name.
nuance: 심지어 introduces an extreme or surprising addition that pushes a point further than you'd expect — 'even', 'on top of that', 'and get this'. It escalates, whether the extra fact is good (맛있고, 심지어 싸다) or bad (춥고, 심지어 비까지 온다), and it characteristically triggers the particle 도 ('also/even') on the following item. Contrast it with 게다가 ('moreover / what's more'): 게다가 simply adds another point on the same level, fairly neutrally, while 심지어 signals that the next fact is the surprising, over-the-top extreme — the one that makes you raise your eyebrows. Compare also 조차/마저 (particles meaning 'even', stressing the least-expected case); 심지어 often works alongside them. The English-speaker pitfall is using 심지어 as a flat 'also' (that's 또/그리고) or swapping it for neutral 게다가, and forgetting the 도 that naturally follows — 심지어 사과도 안 했어요, not 심지어 사과 안 했어요.

usage: I can't understand it at all
examples: 이 문제는 도저히 모르겠어요.
I can't figure out this problem no matter what.
도저히 + 모르겠어요 = total inability after real effort.
너무 매워서 도저히 못 먹겠어요.
It's so spicy I just can't eat it.
도저히 + 못 ...겠어요 conveys giving up despite trying.
도저히 시간을 낼 수가 없어요.
There's just no way I can make time.
도저히 + -ㄹ 수가 없다 = flat impossibility, however hard one tries.
nuance: 도저히 means 'by no means / no matter how hard one tries', and it MUST be paired with a negative — 못, 안, 모르다, or -ㄹ 수 없다 — because its whole job is to intensify an impossibility reached after genuine effort: not just 'I can't', but 'I've tried and there is simply no way'. Without a negative the sentence is ungrammatical (도저히 할 수 있어요 is wrong). Contrast it with 절대 ('never / absolutely (not)'): 절대 can negate too, but it sounds like a firm vow or prohibition about will or principle (절대 안 해 = I absolutely won't, by choice), whereas 도저히 is about practical impossibility despite trying (도저히 못 해 = I genuinely can't manage it). It collocates with 도저히 ~ 수 없다, 도저히 못 ~겠다, 도저히 안 되다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 도저히 in a positive sentence, or reaching for it to mean a willful 'never' where 절대 fits better.

Swapping it for 절대 (never, by will) — 절대 안 해 is a vow of refusal, while 도저히 못 해 is practical inability after trying; the nuance differs.
Forgetting the 'after real effort' meaning — 도저히 implies you genuinely tried and it's impossible, not a casual 'I don't feel like it'.

examples: 기다리느니 차라리 걸어가는 게 빠르겠어요.
Rather than wait, walking would be faster.
-느니 차라리 = 'rather than (doing X)' — the core comparison frame.
복잡한 데 가느니 차라리 집에서 쉴래요.
I'd sooner rest at home than go somewhere crowded.
Sets a disliked option (가느니) against the preferred-but-still-not-ideal one.
택시비 낼 바엔 차라리 일찍 나올게요.
Rather than pay for a taxi, I'll just leave early.
-ㄹ 바엔 차라리 = 'if it comes to (X), I'd rather' — choosing the lesser cost.
nuance: 차라리 picks the lesser of two undesirable options — 'I'd rather', 'I'd sooner', 'better to... instead' — when NEITHER choice is good and you're settling for the more bearable one. The tone is resigned, not enthusiastic: it's a grudging preference, often implying 'this still isn't great, but it beats the alternative'. It characteristically follows the patterns -느니 (차라리) and -ㄹ 바에(는)/-ㄹ 바엔 차라리, both meaning 'rather than doing X', which set up the worse option being rejected. Contrast it with a plain 더 좋다 ('like better'): 더 좋다 is a positive preference between two acceptable things, while 차라리 specifically chooses between two bad-ish things. The English-speaker pitfall is using 차라리 for an option you genuinely want and feel good about — that implies you're happy, which clashes with 차라리's 'lesser evil' resignation; and forgetting that it normally compares against a worse alternative, so it rarely stands alone without that contrast in mind.
